terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see tonight's rope count.

tasks.title: Name the team
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `kit_store.py`, make a variable called `team_name` that holds the text `Brackenridge Mountain Rescue`, then print it.

Check runs your file and reads `team_name` after the lines under `# Task 1`: it must hold exactly that text. Then it looks for the name among the lines those lines print.
nextSteps: Write the name, `=` and the text in quotes.
Print it with `print` on the next line.
Run `python3 kit_store.py` and read the output.
hints: A variable is made with a name, `=` and a value. The lesson shows one for the hall.
The value is text, so it needs quotes. When you print the variable, its name goes without quotes.
Two lines: `team_name = "..."` with the team's name where the dots are, then `print(team_name)`.

tasks.title: Count the ropes
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, make a variable called `ropes_left`. It starts with the number of ropes in the store, which is in `ropes_in_store` near the top of the file. Print it like this, with the number `ropes_left` holds:

```
Ropes in store: 9
```

Check runs your file with other counts in place of the ones at the top, so `ropes_left` has to be built on the name `ropes_in_store`, not on a number you type. Then it looks for that line under `# Task 2`.
nextSteps: Read the two lines under "Tonight's count".
Give it the value of `ropes_in_store` by writing that name.
Print the text and the variable together, then run the file.
hints: A variable can start with the value of another variable, not only with a number or text you type.
On the right of `=`, write the name of the variable that holds the count. `print` can take the text and the variable together, with a comma between them.
`ropes_left = ...` with the store's variable name where the dots are, then `print("Ropes in store:", ropes_left)`.

tasks.title: Take ropes out for a callout
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, `ropes_taken_out` ropes went out on tonight's callout. Give `ropes_left` a new value: the number of ropes left in the store. Then print it like this:

```
Ropes after the callout: 5
```

Check starts Task 3 from `ropes_left` as Task 2 should make it, with other numbers at the top, and reads `ropes_left` after the lines under `# Task 3`. Then it looks for that line.
nextSteps: Under `# Task 3`, start a line with the name `ropes_left` and `=`.
On the right, take `ropes_taken_out` away from what is in the store now.
Print the new count like the task shows it.
Run the file: you should see two different counts.
hints: You are not making a new variable here. You are giving the one you made a new value.
Giving a variable a new value is its name, `=` and the new value. The right side can use the variable's own value from before.
The line has the shape `ropes_left = ropes_left - ...`, with the variable for the ropes that went out where the dots are.

tasks.title: Give x and y real names
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, two variables are called `x` and `y`, and nobody can tell what they hold. Rename `x` to `leader_name` and `y` to `kit_officer_name`, everywhere they appear. Their values stay the same.

Check runs your file and reads `leader_name` and `kit_officer_name` after the lines under `# Task 4`, and makes sure `x` and `y` are gone.
nextSteps: Read the four lines under `# Task 4`.
Rename it where it is used too, then do the same for `y`.
Run the file: it should print the same two lines as before.
hints: A variable's name appears where it is made and everywhere it is used.
If you rename it in one place only, Python stops with a `NameError` that names the one it no longer knows. Read it: it tells you which line to fix.
Four places change: the two lines that make `x` and `y`, and the two `print` lines that use them.
